conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the claim is unsupported by current evidence, noting that while one small study suggested benefit, the gold-standard Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to confirm its efficacy.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
I researched this claim using the available evidence, and it's more accurate to call it "unproven" than outright "false" — but your skepticism is well-founded.

**The main supporting evidence** comes from a single 2010 randomized controlled trial by Manber et al. (Stanford), published in Obstetrics & Gynecology (https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/2010/03000/acupuncture_for_depression_during_pregnancy__a.7.aspx). It found that a specific "depression-specific" acupuncture protocol reduced symptoms more than control acupuncture or massage in 150 pregnant women with major depressive disorder. This is often the sole source cited in popular claims (e.g., https://medicalxpress.com/news/2010-02-acupuncture-lessens-depression-symptoms-pregnancy.html).

**However, this finding has not been robustly replicated.** A follow-up feasibility study explicitly called its own results "preliminary" and noted evidence was "limited to three clinical studies" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4758005/). Most critically, the **Cochrane systematic review** on non-pharmacological interventions for antenatal depression concluded: "There is not enough evidence available to determine if acupuncture... [is an] effective intervention in treating antenatal depression" (https://www.cochrane.org/th/evidence/CD006795_interventions-other-pharmacological-psychosocial-or-psychological-treating-antenatal-depression). Cochrane reviews are considered the gold standard for evidence synthesis and specifically flagged insufficient data.

Related meta-analyses on postpartum (not antenatal) depression similarly report inconclusive or mixed findings across trials of variable quality (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1136/acupmed-2017-011530).

**Conclusion:** The claim overstates the evidence. One small RCT suggested benefit, but the authoritative Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to confirm acupuncture's efficacy for depression during pregnancy. The claim should be labeled "unsupported by current evidence" rather than proven true.
